stories.title: South Korea President Lee backs stronger self-defence, says drills not aimed at North Korea
stories.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urges stronger independent defence of country and supports continuing the transfer of wartime operational control from the US. Lee emphasises the US-South Korea alliance and independent defence as mutually reinforcing and calls for faster development of nuclear-powered submarines. He clarifies that civil defence exercises alongside US-South Korea drills are defensive, aimed at protecting citizens, not threatening North Korea or raising tensions. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called on Aug 18 for stronger independent defence capabilities, while saying annual civil defence exercises coinciding with joint US-South Korea military drills were defensive and not intended to threaten North Korea. The remarks came after US President Donald Trump instructed the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the joint military exercises with South Korea, and said North Korean leader Kim Jong Un had responded to his outreach. Lee said Seoul should proceed without disruption with the planned transfer of wartime operational control from the US during his term, in line with the government’s existing plan. “A strong alliance makes the foundation of security stronger, and strengthening our own capabilities increases our value and necessity as an ally,” Lee said in a Cabinet meeting, describing the US-South Korea alliance and independent defence as mutually reinforcing. He also called for faster progress on South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine programme and for developing officers capable of integrated operations for future conflicts, as distinctions between battlefields become less clear. At a National Security Council meeting on Aug 18, Lee said the civil defence exercises held alongside major US-South Korea military drills were defensive in character, aimed at safeguarding South Koreans’ lives and safety.

stories.title: Make it rain: Indonesia chases clouds to stem El Nino fires
stories.summary: Indonesia is using cloud seeding to fight wildfires worsened by a strong El Nino, with over 285,000 hectares burned in 2026 so far. Cloud seeding aims to trigger rain but is limited by dry conditions and has uncertain effectiveness and environmental concerns. Fires threaten peatlands and rainforests; authorities focus on prevention, enforcement, and peatland restoration to reduce fire risks and regional haze. PALANGKARAYA, Indonesia - Indonesia’s Borneo, home to pristine rainforest and protected species, is burning. Meteorologist Safillah Anggie Wahyuni hopes a solution lies in the clouds. Indonesia believes cloud seeding can help it tackle a wildfire season that experts say is on track to be among the worst in years, driven by a strong El Nino. Indonesia’s government says over 100,000ha burned in the first half of the year. Independent analysis by deforestation monitoring site Nusantara Atlas puts the figure through July at over 285,000ha – more than four times the size of Jakarta. Cloud seeding, which involves sprinkling silver iodide, salts or other particles into clouds to trigger precipitation, is rarely used to tackle wildfires globally. But Indonesia is ramping up efforts, scarred by 2015 fires during a previous strong El Nino that burned through millions of hectares and created a regional haze crisis. “Weather modification does not create clouds: we optimise clouds that have the potential to produce rains,” Safillah told AFP after flying over Palangkaraya in Borneo’s central Kalimantan. “Weather modification will only be effective if the conditions are right,” she added.
